stories.title: Woman Jailed for Helping a Scam Gang That Cheated Singaporeans
stories.headline_kid: A Filipino woman has been sent to jail for helping a scam gang in Cambodia trick people in Singapore out of their money.
summary: Have you heard of a 'scam compound'? It is a place, often overseas, where people are tricked into working for criminals who cheat others out of money using phone calls and messages. This story is about one such place in Cambodia.

A woman from the Philippines told the court that she travelled to Cambodia thinking she had found a normal job. Instead, she discovered she had joined a criminal group, called a syndicate, that was scamming victims in Singapore.

The court did not fully accept her excuse and jailed her because she still took part in the scam activities, even after finding out what was really happening. Her case shows how scam gangs sometimes trick their own workers, not just their victims.

This matters for Singapore because many local victims lose their hard-earned savings to these overseas scam operations every year. Singapore's police keep working with other countries to catch the people behind these crimes.

lenses.me: If you ever see a job advert online that sounds too good to be true, especially one asking you to work overseas, always tell a trusted adult before doing anything.
lenses.family: Parents may want to remind older family members, especially those looking for jobs abroad, to check that companies are real before travelling.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can help each other spot suspicious online job offers or too-good-to-be-true money schemes.
lenses.nation: Singapore works closely with other countries' police forces to track down scam gangs that target Singaporeans, showing how seriously the country takes scam prevention.
lenses.world: Scam syndicates often operate across borders, which means countries must cooperate internationally to stop them.

stories.title: Singapore's Neighbours Fight the Haze With Rain-Making Planes
stories.headline_kid: Indonesia is letting Malaysia fly special planes into its sky to make it rain and clear the haze, while police have arrested 72 people accused of starting the forest fires.
summary: You may remember days when the sky in Singapore looked grey and hazy. That smoky haze usually comes from forest and land fires in Indonesia, blown over by the wind. This week, the haze got so bad that it affected Malaysia too, especially the state of Sarawak on Borneo island.

To help clear the air, Indonesia has given Malaysia special permission to fly planes into its airspace for something called cloud seeding. This is like giving clouds a gentle push to make it rain faster — imagine shaking a fizzy drink bottle a little to make the bubbles rise quicker. Planes spray tiny particles into clouds, which helps raindrops form and fall, washing smoke particles out of the sky.

Meanwhile, Indonesian police arrested 72 people suspected of starting some of the fires. If found guilty, they could face huge fines or up to 15 years in jail, showing how seriously the country now treats deliberate fire-starting.
Singapore also watches the haze situation closely every year, since smoke can drift here too, sometimes affecting the air we breathe and outdoor activities like PE lessons.

lenses.me: If the haze reaches Singapore, you might need to stay indoors during recess or wear a mask outdoors.
lenses.family: Families may need to check the air quality (PSI) readings and keep windows closed on hazy days.
lenses.friends: Outdoor school events like sports day could be postponed if the haze becomes unhealthy.
lenses.nation: Singapore works with Indonesia and Malaysia every year to reduce the effects of transboundary haze on our air quality.
lenses.world: This shows how environmental problems like haze do not stay within one country's borders — they require neighbouring countries to work together.

stories.title: Oil Prices Drop as US Plans Tough Action Against Iran
stories.headline_kid: Oil prices around the world fell after the United States announced its toughest ever economic action against the country of Iran.
summary: Oil is one of the most important things traded around the world. It is used to make petrol for cars, buses and planes, and even plastic for toys. Countries buy and sell oil constantly, and its price can go up or down depending on world events.

The United States said it would launch what it called the 'most crushing' economic action ever against Iran, a country in the Middle East. This means the US wants to stop other countries from trading with Iran, almost like giving Iran a very strict time-out from the world market.

Because of this news, oil prices actually fell instead of rising. Traders were waiting to see the exact details of the plan, and some worried it might reduce how much oil moves around the world in future.

Even though Singapore is far from Iran, changes in oil prices can affect us too. Petrol prices at the pump, bus and taxi fares, and even the price of imported goods can be linked to how expensive oil is around the world.

lenses.me: If petrol prices change, you might notice your family talking about fuel costs when driving or taking a Grab.
lenses.family: Lower or higher oil prices can affect your family's monthly transport budget.
lenses.friends: Not much direct effect, but it's a good topic to discuss how world events connect to daily life.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports all its oil, so global oil price changes affect the cost of living here.
lenses.world: Oil prices affect economies everywhere, showing how connected the world's countries are through trade.

stories.title: Typhoon Narra Floods China and Vietnam
stories.headline_kid: A powerful typhoon called Narra dumped heavy rain on Vietnam and southern China, causing floods and forcing thousands of people from their homes.
summary: A typhoon is a giant spinning storm, similar to a hurricane, that brings very strong winds and heavy rain. This week, a typhoon named Narra swept through northern Vietnam and southern China, causing serious flooding and landslides.

In China's Guangxi region, rising floodwaters forced the government to move about 54,000 people to safety. Of these, over 8,000 people had to stay in emergency shelters because their homes were no longer safe.

The heavy rain also damaged roads, buildings and farm crops, making it harder for people in the affected areas to get around or grow food. Rescue workers used boats to reach people trapped by the rising waters.

Singapore rarely experiences typhoons because we are located near the equator, where these storms usually do not form. However, if your family is planning to travel to Vietnam or China, this kind of news is a good reminder to check weather updates before any trip.

lenses.me: If your family is travelling to a place with a typhoon warning, you might need to change your holiday plans.
lenses.family: Parents may need to check flight and travel advisories before visiting affected areas.
lenses.friends: This is a good topic to bring up during Geography lessons about weather and natural disasters.
lenses.nation: Singapore is fortunate to rarely face typhoons due to its location near the equator, unlike many neighbouring countries.
lenses.world: Scientists say that typhoons and storms may be getting stronger due to climate change, affecting many countries in Asia.

stories.title: Robots Race, Fight and Do Tai Chi at China's 'Robot Olympics'
stories.headline_kid: Human-shaped robots competed in running races, martial arts and even tai chi at a huge robot games in Beijing — and one robot caught fire during its 100m race!
summary: Imagine an Olympics, but instead of athletes, the competitors are robots shaped like humans. That is exactly what happened in Beijing at the World Humanoid Robot Games, a five-day event where humanoid robots competed in sports like sprinting, boxing and even the slow, graceful martial art called tai chi.

The games were not just for fun — they also tested how well robots could handle real-life situations, like working in a simulated factory, serving in a restaurant, or helping during an emergency. Scientists want to see if robots could one day take on jobs that are difficult or dangerous for humans.

Not everything went smoothly. During a 100m race, one robot burst into flames and had to be put out with a fire extinguisher, reminding everyone that this technology is still being tested and improved.

Singapore is also investing in robotics, with delivery robots already seen in some malls and hospitals, and many local schools running robotics clubs and competitions. Events like this in China give us a glimpse of what robots might be able to do in the future.

lenses.me: If you enjoy building or programming things, robotics could be an exciting field to explore in future CCAs or competitions.
lenses.family: Your family might already use robot vacuum cleaners at home — a small taste of the same technology being tested in China.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates could talk about which robot skill (running, fighting, or tai chi) seems the hardest to master.
lenses.nation: Singapore encourages robotics and AI learning in schools, hoping to prepare students for future careers involving smart machines.
lenses.world: Countries like China are racing to develop humanoid robots that could one day change how factories, hospitals and even homes operate.
